To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
controlled hydrolysis of dinuclear titanium-salen complexes led to the isolation of well-defined dinucleating complexes.
the hydrolytic cleavage of donor-substituents in dinuclear Ti(IV) complexes leads to the formation of cytotoxic dinuclear Ti-O-Ti complexes with a μ-oxo-bridge.
controlled hydrolysis of the titanium-salan complexes leads to the formation of dinuclear titanium-oxo species, which are cytotoxic in the low micro molar range.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis, structure determination and biological characterization of donor-substitued titanium-salan complexes.
the development and characterization of dinuclear titanium-salalen complexes with cytotoxic activity.
the synthesis of new dinuclear metal complexes and their characterization by means of spectroscopic techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dinuclear complexes of the type [Ti2(μ-O)(μ-OR)(salen)]2+ (R = H, Me) are the most active cytotoxic species in the series of titanium-salan complexes.
the dinuclear complexes are not the active metabolites of the titanium-salan complexes, but rather the monomeric complexes.
the cytotoxicities of dinuclear titanium-salans are not only comparable but also superior to their mononuclear analogues.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we could show for the first time that dinuclear complexes of titanium-salan can be formed and are cytotoxic, and that these complexes are possible metabolites of titanium(IV)-salan complexes.
we were able to show that dinuclear titanium-salens are cytotoxic in low μM concentrations.
the hydrolysis of the titanium-salan complexes leads to the formation of dinuclear complexes which are highly cytotoxic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cytotoxicity of dinuclear titanium-salen complexes is not only due to the formation of the μ-oxo-bridged dinuclear complexes, but also due to the presence of the labile alkoxide.
controlled hydrolysis of dinuclear titanium-salans can lead to dinuclear complexes with cytotoxic activity.
dinuclear metal-salan complexes are promising candidates for anti-cancer drugs, and that the hydrolysis of mononuclear metal-salan precursors may lead to the generation of such dinuclear complexes.
